The early life stages of Truncilla truncata are marked by precise size thresholds that delineate critical developmental transitions. Newly released glochidia, dispersing from the marsupial gills of the adult, exhibit a remarkably small shell length at birth of 0.02 cm [Lb = 0.02 cm], a dimension typical of unionid larvae that must undergo a brief parasitic encystment on a fish host. Following the parasitic phase and subsequent excystment, the post-larval bivalve settles onto the substrate, at which point the shell length at settlement is recorded as 0.03 cm . This represents the onset of the free-living benthic juvenile stage. The transition from the lecithotrophic larval phase to the onset of exogenous feeding occurs rapidly after settlement, with the juvenile beginning to filter phytoplankton and detrital particles from the water column. These initial size measurements, though extremely small, lay the foundation for a protracted growth trajectory that will continue over several decades in this long-lived freshwater mussel species.

Growth throughout the juvenile and sub-adult phases proceeds steadily, and the species eventually attains a definitive adult body size that appears to be constrained by both physiological limits and habitat conditions. Field surveys and mark-recapture studies on Truncilla truncata indicate that the ultimate shell length approaches 6.5 cm [Li = 6.5 cm] in fully mature individuals, representing the maximum dimension recorded for this taxon across its range. The corresponding asymptotic body mass yields an ultimate wet weight of 9.99 grams [Wwi = 9.99 grams], a value that aligns closely with size-corrected predictions derived from related unionid taxa such as Unio tumidus. This adult mass is relatively modest compared to some larger congeners, reflecting a life-history strategy oriented toward moderate somatic investment and extended reproductive tenure. The attainment of the final shell length typically coincides with a deceleration in annual growth increments, as somatic expansion slows considerably once the individual approaches this upper size limit, with most adults falling within a narrow range of this ceiling.

Reproductive development in Truncilla truncata proceeds over an extended period, with the onset of sexual maturity occurring at a distinct morphological milestone. Histological examination of gonadal tissues and morphometric analysis of shell dimensions reveal that the shell length at puberty is approximately 2 cm [Lp = approximately 2 cm], a size that typically corresponds to an individual age of around 20 years based on growth ring counts and von Bertalanffy growth model fits. This delay in the initiation of gametogenesis is characteristic of many freshwater unionids, which invest heavily in early somatic growth before allocating resources toward reproductive effort. The protracted pre-reproductive phase, spanning nearly two decades, is interpreted as a bet-hedging strategy that reduces the risk of reproductive failure in unpredictable riverine environments. Once this threshold shell length is achieved, the gonads become active and the individual is capable of participating in the species' annual spawning events, marking a transition to the reproductively active adult stage.

At a maintained water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the gestation period from fertilization to the release of mature glochidia is approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days], representing the age at birth for the larval offspring. This relatively rapid brooding duration is typical for unionids that employ a short-term marsupial cycle. The reproductive output of a fully mature female with a shell length of 4.53 cm has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. A female at this size produces approximately 883,889 larvae per spawning season [Ri = approximately 883,889 larvae per spawning season], and typically completes a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = single spawning event per year]. This immense reproductive potential compensates for the high larval mortality typical of the parasitic life stage.

Longevity data for Truncilla truncata, derived from annual growth ring analyses on collected shells and from long-term monitoring of tagged individuals in stable populations, confirm that the species is remarkably long-lived. With a maximum recorded lifespan of 6,935 days [am = 6,935 days] at a water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], which is equivalent to roughly 19 years, Truncilla truncata ranks among the longer-lived unionid species of North American freshwaters. This extended lifespan, combined with the late age at puberty and the high annual fecundity, positions Truncilla truncata as a classic example of a slow-paced, iteroparous life-history strategist. Periodic episodes of low flow and high sedimentation can disrupt recruitment events, but the longevity of the adult population buffers the species against transient environmental stochasticity, allowing individuals to contribute larvae to the population across many successive breeding seasons.
